blocks.text: 英伟达CEO黄仁勋的辞职对美国开放模型生态的发展是一大挫折。英伟达在支持开放模型上仍有财务利益，即避免权力集中在少数客户手中——这些客户会自研芯片，从而削减英伟达的利润；但支持开放生态与其说是一个靠工程手段硬啃就能解决的难题，不如说是一道棘手的谜题。

blocks.text: 众所周知，英伟达的业务运营极度依赖黄仁勋这位掌舵者，因此外界普遍认为前路充满挑战（甚至可能出现更多高调的离职，无论是经由芯片走私调查，还是老套的鲨鱼环伺、觊觎可挖角的人才）。英伟达的头号目标是稳住大局、在未来24个月内向客户交付，并防止崩盘。开放模型一直是黄仁勋较为雄心勃勃的、创始人风格的押注之一。他一直在向这一领域大量注资，而这种投入很可能会枯竭。

blocks.text: 在这一时期，开放模型经济尚处于萌芽阶段。这几年对于确立用例、收入流以及继续训练下一代模型的动机至关重要。我在 Fireworks Forge 最近的演讲中讨论了这些早期年份的敏感性（幻灯片、录音）。核心论点是：开放模型有一个利好、一个值得乐观的理由，以及一个利空。

blocks.text: 利好的一面是，开放模型经济正确地抓住了“智能所有权”和企业后训练这一关键赛道。尚待确定的是下游市场究竟有多大。

inlines.text: 利好的一面是，开放模型经济正确地抓住了“智能所有权”和企业后训练这一关键赛道。尚待确定的是下游市场究竟有多大。

blocks.text: 利空的一面是，在算力如此紧缺的情况下，开放模型作为真正商品化智能的长期真正益处还远未实现。短期内，推理初创公司同样难以获得足够的芯片（因为 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 买走了太多产能），开放权重模型之间的利润竞争微乎其微。如果开源模型也以巨大的推理利润率提供服务——正如我们从 DeepSeek 的 DeepInfer 发布中所了解到的——那它们就远非商品。在这种范式下，拥有更好规模经济、以及从模型到数据中心和芯片一体化整合的闭源实验室将会胜出。我在最近一篇关于开放模型经济的文章中详细阐述了这一挑战。

blocks.text: 民主党政府正大幅增加对主张监管 AI 行业、推动“安全”的候选人的资助。这些人中不少觉得自己必须做点什么，普遍认为开放模型不安全，却并不了解开放模型在收益上的复杂性。我近期最大的担忧是州层面的草率监管，其次是国家级监管。从今年夏天起，我们一直距离一场危机只差一个强大的中国开放权重模型。这一判断至今仍然成立——尤其是我们正进入一个动荡的网络安全新均衡。我们还没有看到由流行的中国开放权重模型驱动的大规模黑客攻击，但这不是会不会发生的问题，而是何时发生的问题。当“开放权重鹰派”开始追猎时，需要有个人来倡导谨慎和生态视角。

blocks.text: 如今推倒开源 AI 的多米诺骨牌很容易——可一旦推倒，再想扭转下游的权力集中、安全研究的减少以及长期创新受到的压制，就难得多。从公开数据看，这像是在长期创新与短期风险之间做权衡，但这是因为开放模型经济实在太难衡量（例如它最有价值的部分跑在私有基础设施上）。这是整个生态和我的工作反复面临的挑战。

blocks.text: 今年夏天 Jacob Coxon 的那场风波也是如此。顶级实验室周围的那套安全文化早已广为人知，但围绕数据中心选对了时机、又借上奥弗顿窗口，就把它变成了全国性议题。开放模型安全也很可能在某个时刻迎来同样的局面，因为驱动现代媒体算法的往往是伤害、风险或安全相关的叙事。我无法想象我在开放科学上的工作能引发这样的媒体周期，因为那永远不会发生。

blocks.text: Jordan Schneider：我确实想听听你们怎么看这件事有多糟——Jensen 如今已不在美国创新的未来牌桌上了。我们也该谈谈开放模型。我是说，他可是最大的旗手，对吧？Dylan，你刚才在说——我还是不太明白，为什么没人干脆花个几十亿美元，做出比 Kimi 或 DeepSeek 更好的东西，然后开源。

Dylan Patel：没那么简单。问题不在钱，而在人才。最有才华的那批人基本都在 Anthropic、OpenAI、DeepMind 和 Meta TBD 工作，对吧？剩下的人则分散在上百家创业公司里。没错，Thinking Machines 的团队确实很强，但它有 Moonshot 那么强吗？没有。论技术水平，Moonshot 大概和美国几家实验室不相上下，只是在算力和部署上差距很大。所以我认为，如果没有规模优势，你就赢不了。没错，这些小实验室在模型上砸了很多钱，可 DeepMind、Grok、Meta 却经常落后于中国实验室的前沿水平，而它们花的钱更多。所以事情不是“哦，花个几十亿美元就能做出更好的模型”这么简单。
最能吸引人才的人，是站在运动最前沿的人。Jensen 推动了这件事，但在很多指标上他仍然处于下风。Nemotron 的雄心够大，人也强，但还没做到能被称为“任务完成”的程度。构建前沿模型的竞争，比大多数人以为的要激烈得多。一个拥有数十亿美元、靠谱的人手和良好氛围的组织，未必就能走到那一步。你通常需要一些特别的东西。

blocks.text: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on.

blocks.text: In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge (slides, recording). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside.

blocks.text: The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is.

blocks.text: The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy.

blocks.text: There’s a major swell in Democratic government funding towards candidates that want to regulate the AI industry, fostering “safety”. Many of these people feel a need to do something and have general opinions that open models are unsafe, while not being educated on the complexities of their benefits. My biggest near-term worry is sloppy regulation at the state level, followed by national regulation. We’ve been one, strong Chinese open-weight model away from a crisis since this summer. It still holds – especially as we enter a new, turbulent equilibrium of cybersecurity. We have not seen a major hack driven by a popular Chinese open-weight model, but it is a matter of when, not if. We need someone to encourage caution and an ecosystem perspective when the “open-weight hawks” come hunting.

We need someone to encourage caution and an ecosystem perspective when the “open-weight hawks” come hunting.

blocks.text: Knocking over the open-source AI domino today is easy — if done, unwinding the downstream concentration of power, reduction in safety research, and stifling of long-term innovation is far harder. On public data, it looks like balancing long-term innovation versus short term risks, but this is due to how horribly hard it is to measure the open model economy (e.g. the most valuable aspects of it run on private infrastructure). It’s a recurring challenge facing the ecosystem and my work.

blocks.text: Jordan Schneider: I do want your guys’ take on just how bad this is, that Jensen’s now off the table for the future of American innovation. And we should talk about open models. I mean, he was the big champion, right? Dylan, you were talking earlier — I still don’t understand quite why someone didn’t just spend a few billion dollars and make something better than Kimi or DeepSeek and open source it.

Dylan Patel: Not that easy. It’s not money, it’s talent, man. All of the most talented people primarily work at Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta TBD, right? And then those who don’t are split across a hundred different startups. I mean, yes, Thinking Machines has a cracked team, but is Thinking Machines as good as Moonshot? No. Moonshot skill-wise is probably just as good as the US labs. They just have a big deficit in compute and deployment. So I think if we don’t have a scale advantage, then you don’t win. Yes, these smaller labs have spent a lot of money on models. But DeepMind, Grok, Meta have regularly fallen behind the frontier of Chinese labs, and they’re spending more. So it’s not just, oh, spend a few billion dollars and you can make a model that’s better.

The best people for attracting talent are the ones at the front of movements. Jensen helped catalyze this, and on many metrics was still losing. Nemotron has had the right level of ambition and strong people, but it hasn’t delivered to the point of being called “mission accomplished.” The competition here in building leading-edge models is more fierce than most give credit to. Having an organization with billions of dollars, solid people, and good vibes may not get you there. You normally need something special.

blocks.text: It could be the case that Thinking Machines has gotten to maturity in its commitment to open models, with its recent Inkling 2 Small being the best Western open-weight model in a while. Still, it’s far behind Kimi K3.1 Pro and expectations are high for Zhipu’s next GLM update. It’s a better sign that we’re at least having this debate, but the open ecosystem is riddled with questions and answers like this – maybe they can pull it off? On the other side of the equation, closed labs like Anthropic look like some of the greatest businesses ever assembled, which inspires confidence in the longevity of their approach.

blocks.text: The fundamental problem is that the open-weight ecosystem needs someone who will pick up the phone to abate a crisis. There are more challenges ahead. The most likely allies we could turn to are from the hyperscalers, the likes of Zuckerberg, Andy Jassy, or Satya. With such a coordinated campaign of pressure from the AI safety community that has open models as a negative target, I worry that being proactive is the only way to stay ahead. Jensen has carried that mantle for about two years, and times were messy before he stepped up clearly in 2025. We’re regressing in the operational capability of our movement, when the stakes and attacks are destined to rise. We open model believers are due some soul-searching and coalition building to construct a new platform. Shoes have been emptied that will never fully be refilled.
